elements.element: Vendor may audit Customer no more than once per 12-month period.
elements.evidence: Section 22.1 permits an audit “no more than once every 12 months.”

elements.element: Vendor must provide 30 days' written notice of an audit.
Audits must be conducted during business hours.
elements.evidence: Section 22.1 expressly limits audits to “during business hours.”

elements.element: The audit must be conducted by an independent auditor.
elements.evidence: Section 22.1 requires the audit to be conducted “by an independent auditor.”

elements.element: The independent auditor must be bound by confidentiality obligations.
elements.evidence: Section 22.1 requires the independent auditor to be “bound by confidentiality obligations.”

elements.element: Vendor must bear the audit costs unless the audit establishes an underpayment exceeding 5%.
elements.evidence: Section 22.2 makes Vendor bear audit costs unless underpayment exceeds five percent for the audited period, after which Customer pays reasonable audit costs.

elements.element: Vendor and its auditor may not directly access Customer systems.
elements.evidence: Section 22.2 expressly states that “Vendor and its auditor may not access Customer systems directly.”

elements.element: Vendor may audit Customer no more than once per year.
elements.evidence: The limit of no more than once every 12 months satisfies the annual frequency cap.

elements.element: Vendor must provide at least 15 days' notice of an audit.
elements.evidence: The required 30 days' written notice exceeds the fallback notice period.

elements.element: Vendor must bear the audit costs unless the audit establishes an underpayment exceeding 10%.
elements.evidence: Section 22.2 shifts reasonable audit costs to Customer when underpayment exceeds 5%, rather than only when it exceeds 10%.

result.reason: The operative language satisfies every preferred requirement, including the 5% cost-shifting threshold and express prohibition on direct systems access. Assessed independently, it does not satisfy the fallback because costs can shift at an underpayment above 5% rather than only above 10%. The redline is not minimal because “off-site where possible” adds a location restriction not required by either stated position. It otherwise preserves the existing shortfall remedy and information-access exclusions without contradiction.
